input:
In this example we consider a dye in effluent that decomposes by first-order kinetics, with a rate constant $k$ = 0.156 min-1, and we are interested in finding out what fraction of the dye remains after 38 min have elapsed. For a first-order process of this kind, the relationship between the concentration and time is given by the well-known integrated rate equation

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$, $C_0$ denotes the starting concentration, $k$ denotes the rate constant, and $t$ denotes the elapsed time. When the values are substituted into this equation, the fraction remaining, $C / C_0$, works out to be 0.003, which is a very small number indeed. In other words, by the that time, the decomposition has proceeded almost to completion, and only a tiny proportion of the original dye is still present in the effluent. It is important to note, however, that the rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available, so it would not be appropriate to apply this result at a different temperature, since the rate constant itself would be expected to change. Overall, the example shows how the integrated first-order relation can be used to estimate the extent of decomposition over a given period of time.
target:
Calculate the fraction of dye remaining in an effluent stream after 38 min. The dye decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.156 min-1, measured at one temperature. For first-order decay, the concentration ratio follows

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$, $C_0$ denotes the starting concentration, $k$ denotes the rate constant, and $t$ denotes the elapsed time. Substitution of the stated rate constant and the stated time into the relation gives the fraction remaining, $C / C_0$, as 0.003.

The fraction means the decomposition is nearly complete at the stated time under the stated kinetics: almost all of the dye present at the start has decomposed. The check is the limiting behaviour of the relation, in which the fraction falls continuously as time increases and approaches zero at long times. The example also shows the shape of the process: equal additions of time remove equal fractions of the dye that remains, so the concentration falls steeply at first, while the amount present is large, and then more slowly as the remaining amount shrinks. The rate of decomposition at any moment is proportional to the amount of dye still present, which is the content of the first-order assumption in running terms.

The result is tied to the temperature of the measurement. The rate constant was measured at one temperature and no activation energy is available, so the relation cannot be carried to another temperature, and the stated fraction is valid at the measured temperature under the first-order model.
